archetype.name: Bubble Team (special-teams-sunk start)
archetype.definition: A club that has finished near .500 the last two seasons and is now running slightly below its own 5-on-5 baseline, with a dreadful power play and penalty kill turning coin-flip nights into losses.

report.headline: Special teams are sinking a start that 5-on-5 play can't fully rescue
report.take:
Columbus is seven games into a season that looks a lot like the two before it, only with the special teams broken. The Blue Jackets are 3-4-0, sixth in the Metropolitan and 27th on the site, with a -5 goal differential. That number is heavier than the record suggests, because one ugly 7-3 loss to Florida carries a lot of it. They are not winning on luck. Two of the three wins came in overtime, but Pts vs Goal Diff sits at a neutral -0.1. The record and the margin agree: a below-average team so far.

The damage is on special teams. The penalty kill is stopping 68% of chances, 29th in the league and 11 points under the league average. The power play converts 11.8%, also 29th. Last season this club killed 76% and scored on 18.9% of power plays, so both units are far below their own recent norms. That points to small-sample noise more than a new identity. The all-situations finishing tells the same story. Skaters are shooting 9.3% against a league 11.3%, and all-situations PDO is 98.6, 22nd. A lot of that missing finishing is on the power play.

The less comfortable part is 5-on-5. Last year Columbus won the shot share and the chance share, with a 51% CF % and 52% xGF %. This year those are 47% and 48.1%, and the team gives up 28.1 shots a game, 23rd. The 5-on-5 PDO of 101.5 is above average, so even-strength results are, if anything, slightly flattered. When the special teams recover, the even-strength game may give some of that back.

Goaltending has been the cushion. Jet Greaves is at a .907 save % with +2.1 GSAx and a shutout, and the group's C+ is the best grade on the roster. Zach Werenski is logging 29.37 minutes a night at +7, and Charlie Coyle leads the forwards with six assists and a .553 xGF %. That is enough to keep Columbus in the bubble conversation once the power play and kill normalize. The forward D+ and blueline D grades say it isn't enough to push them clear of it.

strengths.title: Greaves is outplaying his shot quality
strengths.body: Greaves has started four of the seven games with a .907 save %, +2.1 GSAx and the 1-0 overtime shutout of the Rangers. He ranks 17th on the goalie tab. The team's goalies sit at +2.3 GSAx, mid-league but above the league mean. Last season's +7.8 says this goaltending is more repeatable than the club's lean years were.

strengths.title: Werenski and Coyle drive the top
strengths.body: Werenski is playing 29.37 minutes a game and is +7 with six assists. He is the one blueliner holding up in heavy usage. Coyle matches him with six assists and has the best xGF % among the regular forwards at .553. Both look like real roles rather than hot streaks, and they are the base any recovery is built on.

strengths.title: Center depth is producing goals
strengths.body: Kent Johnson has four goals on 20 shots and Cole Sillinger three, so the scoring isn't resting on one line. Johnson's .44 xGF % says his line gives as much as it gets. Still, a team shooting this far below league average shouldn't lack finishers. As the overall shooting % climbs, this depth should show up more on the scoresheet.

concerns.title: Penalty kill and power play broken
concerns.body: A 68% kill and an 11.8% power play both rank 29th. Together they turn neutral nights into losses. Neither fits recent history: the kill has been 75-79% every season since 2021-22. Expect real improvement, but every week it lasts costs points.

concerns.title: 5-on-5 has slipped from last year
concerns.body: Columbus went from controlling play last season to being out-attempted and out-chanced. The xGF % is .481 against .52 a year ago, and shots against run 1.8 over the league average. With a 5-on-5 PDO of 101.5, even-strength results are slightly flattered, not unlucky. This is the problem that won't fix itself.

concerns.title: Third pair and depth D sinking
concerns.body: Behind Werenski, the blueline grades a D. Gudbranson, Soucy and Christiansen rank 204th, 218th and 225th on the defense tab, with xGF % marks of .442, .41 and .393. Opposing wingers are scoring 0.6 points a game above expectation, 23rd in the league, which fits a team losing its defensive-zone battles. Severson's return from missed games helps, but the bottom four is the soft spot.

trend.note: Columbus has alternated wins and losses all month, never winning two straight and never losing more than two. The last five (2-3-0, 0.4 points %) sit a shade under the season rate, with scoring down to 2.2 a game.

weekAhead.headline: A special-teams test, a contender, then the league's weakest offense
weekAhead.body:
Three games spread across the week. The first two are at home against very different opponents, then a trip to Philadelphia. Toronto is 21st on the site but dangerous in exactly the wrong place for Columbus: a 26.7% power play meets a 68% kill. On the other side, a 96.4% Toronto kill meets an 11.8% Columbus power play. At 5-on-5 the Leafs are worse than Columbus, with a .444 xGF % and 29.2 shots against a game. Win that game at even strength and stay out of the box.

Vegas is the real test. They are 8-2-0, third on the site, with A+ forwards and the league's best goal differential. Their defense holds centers 0.94 points under expectation, third in the league, which hits Columbus's center-heavy group. Their one soft spot is a 73.9% kill, a rare chance for the Columbus power play. Philadelphia closes the week at 1-6-3. The Flyers are last in xGF % and shots against, and 31st in shots for. Their goalies (+4.1 GSAx) have kept things closer than the play. Two winnable games and one long shot make four points a fair target.

keyMatchups.title: Columbus PK vs Toronto's power play
keyMatchups.body: Toronto converts 26.7% of power plays, seventh in the league, against a Columbus kill ranked 29th. Toronto's own kill is the league's best at 96.4%, so special teams could swing this game by a goal or more. Columbus needs a low-penalty game to play to its 5-on-5 edge.

keyMatchups.title: Vegas shuts down centers
keyMatchups.body: Vegas holds centers 0.94 points a game under their averages, third-best in the league. Fantilli, Coyle, Johnson and Sillinger carry much of Columbus's offense, so that is a direct hit. The Vegas kill at 73.9% (24th) is the opening if the Columbus power play can finally convert.

keyMatchups.title: Philadelphia can't generate offense
keyMatchups.body: The Flyers rank last in xGF % at .34, last in shots against, and 31st in shots for. That should flip the shot share Columbus has been losing. Their goalies at +4.1 GSAx and a 6.6% shooting % mean the score may stay tighter than the play, so Columbus has to finish.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the penalty kill survives Toronto's power play. If it can't hold there, the 68% is more than early noise.

restOfSeason.body:
With 75 games left, the current pace of 70 points means little. It treats a 29th-ranked penalty kill and 9.3% shooting as permanent, and recent history says otherwise. Expect the kill to settle around 74-79% and scoring to rise toward 2.75-3.15 goals a game as shooting recovers. That alone moves Columbus back toward the .500-ish team of the last two years. What is less likely to bounce back is the 5-on-5 control: the shot and chance shares are below even, and the 101.5 5-on-5 PDO has room to fall.

The likely result is a team near the bubble but on its wrong side: 33-40 wins and 78-90 points. Greaves's goaltending keeps the floor up, while thin depth on defense and middling forward grades cap the ceiling. A real playoff push would need the 5-on-5 numbers to return to last season's 52% chance share, not just better special teams.
swingFactors: Penalty kill returning to its recent mid-70s level

confidence.note: Seven games; special-teams and shooting rates are especially noisy this early.
